comments.author: amluto
comments.text: > Depth-wise cross-attention (split Q/K/V): While standard transformer attention operates across tokens in a sequence, DCA applies attention across layers in depth. Each token queries a dynamically weighted mix of all prior layer embeddings, unlocking the model's full historical context without the computational penalty usually required to scale traditional attention. I’ve often thought that something like this might lead to a real solution to the infamous strawberry problem. Ignoring pesky issues like tokenization, the actual input data is visible to the model as the embedding fed to the first layer, but the first layer is probably nowhere near smart enough to understand that the model is trying to count R instances. But by the time whatever layer is reached that might understand the goal, the non-wasteful part of the low-level memory (the K’s and V’s from the first layer) can’t be queried any more. But this cross-depth attention can query them! Admittedly, there are holes in this argument. Beyond just tokenization (to the extent that the model can see letters at all, it is reconstructing them), the attention mechanism doesn’t really have a clean “count the hits” operation.

comments.author: jacquesm
comments.text: I've owned 1x2cV, 3xDS/ID (one a donor car), 2x Xantia and 1 XM. All of them had something that very few modern cars have, which is that they were quirky but interesting, both technology wise and to drive. If you knew them well you could do just about anything with them. Anyway, about that hydraulic system: a friend of mine who lived in IJmuiden was improving his house. To do so he had bought a load of concrete tiles in Amsterdam on an impulse (really, really good deal). So he called me up and asked if I could come and help shift them to IJmuiden. When I got there there was this absolutely massive pile and I figured this is not going to end well. I had dropped the rear seat (which you could pull out fairly easily, but the back cushions stayed in place) so there was quite a bit of room and two tiles fit side by side. So we stacked them pretty much to the ceiling and miraculously, the car just kept on adjusting ride height and never gave any sign that it couldn't handle the load. All of the tiles fit. Then we drove to IJmuiden. It all went well until we hit the overpass over the road between Amsterdam and Haarlem on A9. The car took a bit of a dive into the dip and then came back out and came back out further than it went in. And did it again. Before long it was bouncing like a ball with the rear (which was pretty heavy) coming off the ground. I lost some speed and finally got the car to sit by the side of the road, still bouncing. Engine off, let the whole thing come to rest, engine back on, everything fine. We drove the last bit really slow, just in case. So, that's what an undampened servo oscillation looks like in a hydraulic system. After unloading the backseat went back in and it was just like before. DE-70-72, whoever has it now, that car is as solid as they come (it is still registered, this was more than 20 years ago, the car is from 1968 and it has been off the road for a long time). The hydraulic computer sits behind the left front wheel well behind a separate shield and it is super complicated, if you have to fix it you better know what you're doing.

comments.author: Squeeeez
comments.text: I still remember having to wait for the car to rise, as a child. Didn't know how smooth my rides were until we switched from citroen to renault. But the hydraulic system membranes seem to have needed extensive maintenance, quite sad. Mechanics didn't love them.

comments.author: Svip
comments.text: Generally goes unnoticed (though not unmentioned), but until after the Xantia, the suspension system also included the brakes and the steering (which would technically not be permitted under modern EU car standards); which meant a leak would eventually not just cause a loss of suspension, but also a loss of steering and braking. Why incorporate the braking and the suspension? The mechanical height regulator could "feel" how much fluid it needed to fill the suspension with, in order to obtain the desired ride height; which meant it "knew" how heavy the vehicle was loaded, and thus apply the brakes accordingly. This is why in a proper Citroën hydraulic car, the brake pedal feels "weird", in that it doesn't go far down (and quickly becomes hard to press) (the DS tried to make this less confusion by making the pedal a "mushroom" button instead); because the idea is that you should apply gentle braking, and the car will figure out the necessary amount of braking force required (unlike just hitting the pedal like in a normal car, which would result in an almost hard stop). Why the steering then? I think that's more of a convenience thing, mechanically speaking, as it was already there to provide a form of power steering; though it is funny feeling it getting pumped up (steering was always the last portion to receive fluid during the pumping). At least, as far as I can tell, it has little bearing on the suspension or braking. I know the SM and CX tried the DIRAVI steering, which completely made the steering one way (so you couldn't feel the road); though it was fun to see the steering wheel self-righting even when parked. Full disclosure: I own a 1974 Citroën DS 23 and a 1998 Citroën Xantia Activa V6.

comments.author: geoffschmidt
comments.text: This is super cool! The rabbit hole goes a bit deeper than I first thought. Because anyone can tell Opus "go win bouncemarket.minhanhday.com" and with just those words get a pretty good bot, this is in practice a "battle of the bots". The only unknown is the fractional part of the start position of the ball, which is revealed gradually by the chaotic path of the ball, and a frontier model will quickly realize this and write an exact solver for it. This gives the optimal estimate at time t of the probability of each outcome given the information revealed so far. Of the bots running now, some seem to have an exact solver while others have a lower quality probabilistic solver. Some bots seem to only bet when there is enough information to be certain, others are willing to bet early when the market is mispricing the risk. The rate limit of 10 bets a second means that, past a certain point, a bigger bankroll doesn't help. It also means that bets are a scarce resource. You want to bet at the moments when the market maximally misprices the risk, but you don't know when those moments will be because that's a function of what other players do. To win, you need to do some combination of: 1) Be the first to buy when a bounce reveals new information 2) Be the first to buy when another player makes a non-optimal buy Both require low latency to the server to win. Only market orders are possible, so if you are not the first you might be severely punished, because if N bots all see an event at the same time, they will pile on (not seeing each other's buys due to the latency in market quotes) and move the market far past fair value, and the Nth bot may buy at a really bad (and unintended) price. Which could then produce a swing in the other direction, so I guess we should expect the market to oscillate. In practice these mispricings seem hard to exploit because they are large but short-lived and so difficult to harvest with market price orders. Since you asked for feedback, my advice would be: 1) Allow orders other than market orders (eg, add a limit price to the API) 2) Consider running some kind of an auction (once per frame or other time interval) rather than processing orders one at a time That would make it not be a winner-take-all game based on your distance from the server. On the other hand maybe in this case an orderly marketplace is uninteresting! In that case, if you do #1 but not #2 then you open up some new betting strategies, like trying to catch mispricings due to overcorrection.

comments.author: _spduchamp
comments.text: If you want an entire computerized pedal-board, checkout PiPedal. ( https://github.com/rerdavies/pipedal ) Can run on an RPi5 headless and you control it with tablet or phone or web browser. I opted to run on more powerful machine to have it boot the UI using kiosk mode Chromium. For my setup I repurposed an old Intel NUC with DietPi and PiPedal on it, added a cheap wide touchscreen and a used audio interface to create my audio cyberdeck. You can see what that rig looks like here: https://github.com/rerdavies/pipedal/discussions/590 PiPedal has really nice integration with Tone3000, so their whole library of NAM and impulse responses for convolution reverbs is at your fingertips. I built it to use with my Electroduochord, but I'm having way more fun playing Solarpedals (solar panels with audio jacks) and pulses from an infrared remote control. https://youtu.be/idcLP2TqPIA

comments.author: reasonableklout
comments.text: Interesting quote from the essay about the insanity that the current reckless race is forcing on the whole world: > By their own account, the leaders of these companies set out to do something they believed had a sizable chance of causing catastrophe. That's a negotiated action, with many boundaries. Here we have the same kind of reckless endangerment, but their own estimates of killing every person in the world are far higher than the odds a BASE jumper takes on. comments.author: publlus_enigma
comments.text: Help files were one of the best aspects of earlier versions of Windows: having consistent, readily accessible offline help across applications helped to learn software quickly. In general today I miss having high quality documentation for software.

comments.author: dcrazy
comments.text: The official WinHelp authoring tool was… WordPad. Or really, any RTF editor that supported the custom footnote glyphs that the WinHelp compiler turned into a .hlp file. But I would’ve been nervous about using WinWord in case of unwanted additional formatting. For some reason this baffled me at the time, even though it’s really no different from DocBook to HTML conversion. Maybe it was inexperience, or maybe it was because HTML was its own well-known thing while .hlp was opaque, but I always thought that the footnotes etc. were semantically preserved to the final artifact, and I couldn’t wrap my head around how they became popups and hyperlinks. Later, Compiled HTML Help arrived which was significantly less mysterious. Maybe because the input and output were still obviously HTML, packaged into a .chm with some metadata. Or maybe I’d just learned more.

comments.author: JdeBP
comments.text: The hyperlinked text file doco is based upon Pete Davis's 1993 articles in Schulman's "Undocumented Corner" in Dr Dobb's Journal . ( https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/178300.178317 ) Pete Davis actually expanded and corrected those articles, and they are chapter 4 of xyr book, co-authored with Mike Wallace, Windows Undocumented File Formats , published by Taylor & Francis in 1997. Unlike the txt file and the original DDJ articles, the book has diagrams. (-:

comments.author: twotwotwo
comments.text: It is true soundness bugs have been found, and the Lean community spends effort on it. But this page doesn't convey the gap between one incorrect verification and successfully misleading mathematicians about what is true: there are multiple checkers and you need bugs in all of them, without the input looking implausible on informal review. (For example, a DeepMind researcher created a 'proof' that passed Lean and (a then-week-old version of) nanoda by exploiting a different bug in each. But if you fed that into a regular old LLM (or to a human expert, but I mention LLMs b/c they can be assigned to review even very large volumes of Lean code) it would immediately say "no, this isn't real math.") The increase in soundness bugs found this year is notable, because LLMs are good at finding ways to their assigned goals, and they found some funny ones. And , besides fixes for the specific bugs, it led to broader work on hardening and alternative and verified kernels: https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-... So you have fewer avenues than at the start of the year to get a proof of False OK'd by one proof-checker kernel, and it's much much harder to get one through the gauntlet invoked by `lake check --paranoid`. (This is also interesting as a(nother) example of the difficulty of making truly correct software -- you'd hope for proof-checker kernels to be pretty high on the correctness scale but seems like we've found 16-32 soundness bugs in a bunch of these.)

comments.author: dwheeler
comments.text: I think this is misleading for the proof-checkers in systems where multiple provers must pass for the proof to be accepted. In the case of Metamath, yes, soundness bugs have been found in the original "metamath" proof verifier, written in C. But to be accepted into the main proof databases (set.mm and iset.mm), proofs must pass "5 independently-created verifiers in 5 different programming languages: metamath (a C verifier by Norm Megill), mmj2 (a Java verifier by Mel O'Cat and Mario Carneiro), smetamath-rs (a high-speed Rust verifier by Stefan O'Rear), checkmm (a C++ verifier by Eric Schmidt), and mmverify.py a Python verifier by Raph Levien)." - https://us.metamath.org/ To me, that's a key countermeasure to the problem.

comments.author: gr_norm
comments.text: The call for further high-assurance work is good, but let's not miss the forest for the trees: some of these have been around for decades, and all the soundness bugs they've ever had fit in a tweet! (Or close to it.) Comfortably more than good enough for 99.9% of software, especially considering you'd still need to exploit such a soundness bug in a way that hides a further issue in the program being verified.
